Presheaves and cocompletions in formal category theory
Nathanael Arkor, Dylan McDermott

Abstract
. We study the relationship between presheaf constructions and free cocompletions in the context of formal category theory, elucidating the coincidence between the two concepts in familiar settings. We show that, in a virtual equipment satisfying mild assumptions, free cocompletions under classes of weights are exhibited by presheaf constructions. We furthermore extend the theory of weighted colimits from enriched category theory to this setting, developing the concepts of atomicity and rank, and providing recognition theorems for presheaf objects, free cocompletions, and cocomplete objects. As an application of our methods, we construct free cocompletions, under arbitrary classes of colimit-small weights, of (possibly large) categories enriched in (not necessarily symmetric) monoidal categories and bicategories; this resolves a longstanding omission in the literature on enriched category theory.

1.
Introduction

The construction of the category of presheaves
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}\mathrel{:=}{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
on a locally small category
{\mathbf{A}}
is perhaps the most fundamental construction in category theory. When
{\mathbf{A}}
is small, the presheaf construction is characterised by two important universal properties.

(1)

It classifies distributors (a.k.a. profunctors or bimodules), in the sense that functors
{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{B}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
are in natural bijection with distributors
{\mathbf{A}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{B}}
.

(2)

It is the free cocompletion of
{\mathbf{A}}
, in that (a)
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
admits all small colimits, and (b) functors
{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{X}
, for
\mathbf{X}
admitting small colimits, are in pseudo natural equivalence with functors
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}\to\mathbf{X}
that preserve small colimits.

When
{\mathbf{A}}
is large, the situation is more subtle. While
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
still classifies distributors, it no longer exhibits the free cocompletion of
{\mathbf{A}}
. However, we may obtain the free cocompletion by restricting
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
to the full subcategory spanned by the
small presheaves
, i.e. the small colimits of representable presheaves. More generally, for any class
\Phi
of
colimit-small weights
(here meaning a class of distributors satisfying an appropriate size condition), corresponding to a class of colimit shapes, the free cocompletion of
{\mathbf{A}}
under
\Phi
-weighted colimits may be obtained as a full subcategory of
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
by restricting to the
\Phi
-weighted colimits of representable presheaves.

For enriched categories, there is a similar story, though additional care is required. For one, given an arbitrary monoidal category
\mathbf{V}
and a
\mathbf{V}
-enriched category
{\mathbf{A}}
, it may not be possible to form the
\mathbf{V}
-category of presheaves
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
, even assuming
{\mathbf{A}}
is small. For another, even supposing we may form
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
, it is not necessarily constructed as a
\mathbf{V}
-category of contravariant
\mathbf{V}
-functors from
{\mathbf{A}}
to
\mathbf{V}
(indeed, for
\mathbf{V}
to itself form a
\mathbf{V}
-category requires
\mathbf{V}
to be closed, and to construct opposites of
\mathbf{V}
-categories requires some form of symmetry on
\mathbf{V}
). However, as long as
\mathbf{V}
is sufficiently nice
1
1

1

For instance,
[
Kel82
]
assumes that
\mathbf{V}
is a complete and cocomplete symmetric closed monoidal category, and we will show in
??
that these assumptions can be substantially weakened.
, it is nevertheless again true that we may form free cocompletions (and, more generally,
\Phi
-cocompletions) of
\mathbf{V}
-categories by restricting to subcategories of
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}

[
Kel82
]
.

This intimate relationship between presheaf constructions and free cocompletions is highly useful in practice, as it gives a simple concrete construction of an a priori entirely abstract object. Furthermore, the knowledge that free cocompletions are exhibited by categories of presheaves allows one to deduce important properties of free cocompletions that are not evidently derivable merely from their universal property. It is therefore desirable to understand how presheaf constructions relate to free cocompletions in general, permitting these techniques to be extended to settings beyond that of categories enriched in a nice monoidal category.

To explain what we mean by
presheaf construction
and
free cocompletion
in general, we recall the philosophy of
formal category theory

[
Gra74
,
SW78
,
Woo82
]
. Category theory provides an expressive language with which to describe totalities of structures and their relationships. Formal category theory arises when we apply the principles of category theory to category theory itself, studying the totalities of categories – as well as variants such as enriched categories, internal categories, and fibred categories – using (two-dimensional) category theoretic techniques. While several frameworks for formal category theory have been proposed, in recent years the formalism of
virtual equipments
has emerged as a particularly apposite setting in which to carry out formal category theory
[
CS10
,
AM24
,
AM25
,
AM25a
,
Kou24
]
.

A virtual equipment is a two-dimensional structure that axiomatises the totality of (large, enriched) categories, functors, distributors, and natural transformations. A virtual equipment has two kinds of morphism:
tight-cells
(denoted
\to
), which axiomatise functors; and
loose-cells
(denoted
{\mathrel{\to}}
), which axiomatise distributors. They thus extend the concept of a 2-category by regarding distributors also as a primitive notion. It is possible to define notions of
presheaf object
and
weighted colimit
in a virtual equipment
[
AM25a
,
AM24
,
Kou24
]
, which recover the usual notions of enriched category theory when instantiated in appropriate virtual equipments of enriched categories. We may therefore ask to what extent the relationship between presheaf constructions and free cocompletions, known classically to hold for categories enriched in nice monoidal categories, holds purely formally.

In this paper, we introduce the notions of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object
and
\Phi
-cocompletion
in a virtual equipment, for
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
a class of loose-cells and
\Phi
a class of weights, and study their relationship. In doing so, we extend much of the classical theory of presheaves and cocompletions – such as atomicity, rank, and recognition theorems – from enriched categories to formal category theory. Our central result,
??
, gives a construction of
\Phi
-cocompletions via presheaf objects, establishing that the classical relationship between presheaves and cocompletions is not specific to enriched categories, but holds for entirely formal reasons.

To demonstrate the utility of our development, we apply our results in the setting of categories enriched in a
normal virtual bicategory
(a structure simultaneously generalising a unital multicategory and a bicategory). While the theory of categories enriched in a monoidal category is well developed
[
Kel82
]
, the theory of categories enriched in multicategories
[
Lam69
]
or in bicategories
[
Wal81
,
Str83
]
is much less mature, despite the abundance of motivating examples
[
Wal82
,
BCSW83
,
Gar14
,
GP18
]
. For a normal virtual bicategory
{\mathbb{V}}
satisfying some mild assumptions, we show that it is possible to construct
\Phi
-cocompletions of
{\mathbb{V}}
-enriched categories via enriched presheaf categories. In particular, when
{\mathbb{V}}
is a bicategory, we have the following.

Theorem

(
)
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a locally complete and locally cocomplete bicategory with right lifts and let
\Phi
be a class of colimit-small weights. For every
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
(not assumed to be small), the free cocompletion of
{\mathbf{A}}
under
\Phi
-weighted colimits exists, and is given by the largest sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of small presheaves on
{\mathbf{A}}
that is closed under
\Phi
-weighted colimits and representable presheaves.

Despite the historical maturity of bicategory-enrichment, which dates back to the 1980s (originating in
[
Wal81
]
’ observation that sheaves may be seen as categories enriched in a bicategory
[
Wal81
,
Wal82
]
), the construction of arbitrary
\Phi
-cocompletions appears to be entirely new; we give a survey of free cocompletions of enriched categories in
??
. In fact, many of the results throughout this paper, which extend the classical theory of colimits and cocompletions for categories enriched in symmetric monoidal categories
[
Kel82
]
to the context of formal category theory, appear to be new even when instantiated in the setting of enrichment in a non-symmetric monoidal category. Our paper may be thus be seen as a contribution to the theory of non-symmetric monoidal and bicategorical enrichment, of independent interest to our formal development.

In the future, we intend to apply this framework to situations beyond enriched categories. There are numerous examples in the literature of category-like structures that admit notions of presheaf construction and free cocompletion, which satisfy the same kinds of theorems as in enriched category theory, and yet have heretofore been studied on a case-by-case basis (necessarily, as no general theory existed). For instance, in each of the following examples, a notion of cocompletion is constructed for a category-like structure by considering an appropriate notion of presheaf construction.

•

For internal categories, there are at least two notions of presheaf construction, depending on one’s attitude to size. For instance,
[
Str80
,
Web07
]
consider exponentials of internal full subcategories (playing the role of an internal ‘category of sets’), whereas
[
Joh02
, §B2.5]
considers a presheaf
indexed category
on an internal category.

•

[
IK86
]
show that, for a small monoidal category
\mathbf{A}
, the convolution monoidal structure on the category of presheaves
{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
exhibits it as the free mononoidal cocompletion of
\mathbf{A}
; this is generalised to pseudo algebras for certain pseudomonads by
[
Wal19
]
.

•

In
[
GL12
]
,
[
GL12
]
develop the theory of
lex colimits
, which is the theory of cocompletions for finitely complete enriched categories, and show that many notions of exactness in category theory are thereby captured.

•

[
Bun13
,
Shu13
]
independently introduced the notion of
indexed enriched
(a.k.a.
enriched indexed
) categories, providing a simultaneous generalisation of indexed categories and enriched categories. In particular,
[
Shu13
]
exhibits free cocompletions of indexed enriched categories via a presheaf construction.

•

In
[
GL20
]
,
[
GL20
]
develop the theory of presheaves and cocompletions for restriction categories, which are axiomatisations of categories of partial functions
[
CL02
]
.

Our expectation is that these arise, for appropriate choices of virtual equipment, as instances of the formal theory of presheaves and cocompletions we develop herein, permitting the general theory to be applied immediately in these settings and facilitating comparison between them.

1.1.
Outline of the paper

In
??
, we recall the definition of virtual equipment and develop some of the basic formal category theory that will be used throughout the paper, focusing on the calculus of right lifts. This may be viewed as an extension of the material in
[
AM24
, §3]
(though familiarity with that work is not assumed here). In
??
, we introduce the notion of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object
, for a class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of loose-cells in a virtual equipment, and study its properties, showing it to satisfy the usual properties satisfied by full subcategories of enriched presheaf categories. In
??
, we introduce the notion of
atomicity
, which generalises the concept of a finitely presentable object in a category, and show how it can be used to characterise presheaf objects. In
??
, we introduce the notion of
rank
, which generalises the concept of a finitary functor. Rank is fundamental to
??
, in which we introduce the concept of a
\Phi
-cocompletion
in a virtual equipment and study its properties, showing it to satisfy the usual properties satisfied by enriched cocompletions. Our formal development culminates in
??
, in which we establish sufficient conditions under which presheaf objects in virtual equipments exhibit free cocompletions. (Naturally, while we have spoken so far only about cocompletions under classes of colimits, the theory of completions under classes of limits is entirely dual: for completeness, we discuss this in
??
.)

To demonstrate the utility of our framework, we use our central result to construct in
??
free (co)completions, under arbitrary classes of (co)limit-small weights, of categories enriched in normal virtual bicategories. The general theory of sections
2
–
8
is then immediately applicable. We conclude in
??
by giving various examples of cocompletions of categories enriched in bicategories.
??
provides some basic material on local completeness and local cocompleteness for virtual double categories, which is used in
??
.

1.2.
Referencing convention

Throughout, we frequently annotate our results with references to comparable results in standard accounts (e.g. in
[
Kel82
]
). ‘Comparable’ here is intended loosely: it is typically the case that, even when specialised to the setting of enriched categories, our results are more general than those we reference, and the proofs we give simpler by virtue of the formal setting in which we work. The references are intended rather to make it convenient for readers of those texts to find a formal analogue (or generalisation) of a given result in the setting of ordinary or enriched categories.

1.3.
Related work

The relationship between distributors, presheaf constructions, and free cocompletions is of historical significance, as it provides the motivation for the three primary approaches to formal category theory in the literature.
[
SW78
]
’ formalism of
Yoneda structures

[
SW78
]
is an axiomatisation of the presheaf construction.
[
Web07
]
showed that, under strong assumptions (holding, for instance, for internal categories, but not for enriched categories), if the presheaf objects on small objects in a Yoneda structure are cocomplete, then they form free cocompletions
[
Web07
,
Kou24
]
. Crucially, cocompleteness is assumed rather than derived (though specific examples are given where this assumption does hold
[
Web07
, §7]
).

[
Woo82
]
’s formalism of
proarrow equipments

[
Woo82
]
, as well as the later
virtual equipments
of
[
CS10
]
and the
augmented virtual equipments
of
[
Kou24
]
, are axiomatisations of the structure of distributors.
[
Kou24
]
introduced presheaf constructions in the setting of augmented virtual equipments, established that this setting generalises that of Yoneda structures
[
Kou24
, §4.34]
, and proved that, under mild assumptions, every presheaf object exhibits a free cocompletion with respect to a class of weighted diagrams. This result is closely related to our central result. However, the universal property that we consider – which is double categorical in nature, rather than merely 2-categorical – is significantly stronger than that of
[
Kou24
]
, and is necessary to generalise important classical theorems about enriched cocompletions to the formal setting. We give a more detailed comparison to
[
Kou24
]
’s work in
??
.

[
BF99
]
demonstrated that
lax-idempotent pseudomonads
, conceived by
[
Koc67
,
Zöb76
]
to axiomatise free cocompletions, also provide a setting for formal category theory. It was shown by
[
Wal18
]
that every lax-idempotent pseudomonad induces a Yoneda structure; in particular, the formal category theory of lax-idempotent pseudomonads is subsumed by that of virtual equipments. Conversely, we show in
??
that every class of weights in a virtual equipment induces a lax-idempotent relative pseudomonad.

2.
Formal category theory in a virtual equipment

We begin by recalling the basic concepts of formal category theory in a virtual equipment, including weighted colimits, (pointwise) extensions, and relative adjunctions. This section is based on
[
AM24
, §3]
, though we generalise several of the definitions and results therein – for instance, by considering colimits weighted by chains of loose-cells, rather than individual loose-cells. Familiarity with
[
AM24
]
is not assumed.

2.1.

A
virtual equipment

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}

the juxtaposition of identity 2-cells:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}

Composition of 2-cells is required to be associative and unital in the evident manner
[
CS10
, Definition 2.1]
: associativity is implicit in pasting diagrams.

Example 2.2

(label=Cat)
.

The virtual double category
\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
is defined as follows.

(2.2.(1))

The underlying category is the category of locally small categories and functors.

(2.2.(2))

A loose-cell from
A
to
B
is a distributor from
{\mathbf{A}}
to
{\mathbf{B}}
, i.e. a functor
{\mathbf{B}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}\times{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}
.

(2.2.(3))

A 2-cell with the following frame

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{A}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{A}_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\mathbf{B}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

comprises a family of functions

\phi_{a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}}\colon p_{1}(a_{0},a_{1})\times\cdots\times p_{n}(a_{n-1},a_{n})\to q(f(a_{0}),f^{\prime}(a_{n}))

for each
a_{0}\in|\mathbf{A}_{0}|,\dots,a_{n}\in|\mathbf{A}_{n}|
, satisfying naturality conditions
[
AM24
, Definition 8.1]
.

The identity 2-cell on a distributor is given by the family of identity functions, and the composition of 2-cells is induced by functoriality of the cartesian product of sets.

In contrast to 2-categories, which admits three notions of dual, there is a single notion of dual for virtual double categories, which for the virtual double category
\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
incorporates both the 2-category
\mathbf{Cat}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
and the bicategory
\mathbf{Dist}{}^{\mathrm{op}}
.

Example 2.3

(
[
AM24
, Definition 2.12]
)
.

The
dual

\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
of a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
is the virtual double category with the same objects and tight-cells as
\mathbb{X}
, for which a loose-cell
A{\mathrel{\to}}B
in
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
is a loose-cell
B{\mathrel{\to}}A
in
\mathbb{X}
, and for which a 2-cell with the frame on the left below in
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
is a 2-cell with the frame on the right below in
\mathbb{X}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{n}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}

The virtual double categories in which we shall be interested satisfy several important properties. The first is the ability to restrict loose-cells along tight-cells: this axiomatises the restriction of distributors along functors.

In this case, we call
p
the
restriction

q(f,g)
.
If
q
is a loose-identity
A(1,1)
(see
??
), we denote
p=A(1,1)(f,g)
simply by
A(f,g)
. For a tight-cell
f\colon A\to B
, the restriction
{B(1,f)\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}B}
, when it exists, is the
companion
of
f
; and the restriction
{B(f,1)\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}A}
, when it exists, is the
conjoint
of
f
. A loose-cell is
representable
if it is the companion of some tight-cell; and
corepresentable
if it is the conjoint of some tight-cell.

Example 2.5

(label=restriction-in-Cat)
.

The restriction of a distributor
q\colon{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}
along functors
f\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}
and
g\colon{\mathbf{B}}\to{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}
in
\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
is the distributor
q(f,g)\mathrel{:=}(a,b)\mapsto q(f(a),g(b))
.

Note that a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
admits restrictions if and only if
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
does
[
AM24
, Lemma 2.14]
.

The second property we shall be interested in is the existence of identity loose-cells, corresponding to the hom-set distributors
{\mathbf{A}}({-},{-})\colon{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}\times{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}
. While virtual double categories do not in general admit composites of loose-cells, we may identify the existence of composites via a universal property.

Definition 2.6

(
[
DPP06
,
CS10
]
)
.

if any 2-cell

Left-composites are unique up to isomorphism and are left-associative in the sense that there is a canonical isomorphism,

(1)

q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{2}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\cong(\cdots(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{2})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}

(2)

Dual statements hold for right-composites, a left-composite in

. We reserve no notation for nullary left- or right-composites, since we shall not make use of them here (all loose-identities we consider have the full universal property of

The ambient setting for formal category theory within which we shall work in this paper is that of a
strict virtual equipment
.

Definition 2.10

(
[
CS10
, Definition 7.6]
)
.

A
virtual equipment
is a virtual double category that admits all loose-identities and restrictions.

Definition 2.11

(
[
AM25a
, Definition 5.1]
)
.

A virtual equipment is
strict
if it is equipped with a strictly functorial choice of restrictions, in the sense that the following 2-cells exhibit the chosen cartesian 2-cells (so that
p(1,1)=p
and

), for all objects
A,A^{\prime},B,B^{\prime\prime}
, tight-cells

.

Note that strictness is a mild assumption: every virtual equipment is equivalent to a strict virtual equipment
[
AM25a
, Theorem A.1]
, and examples of virtual equipments that arise in practice (for instance,
\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
) tend to be strict. Furthermore, strictness is a useful assumption, as it generally allows us to reason about universal properties involving restrictions up to isomorphism rather than up to equivalence (this permits our definition of presheaf object in
??
to have a strict universal property, for instance, which simplifies calculations considerably).

2.2.
Lifts and extensions

Next, we shall explain how limits and colimits in categories are expressed in a virtual equipment. We shall be concerned in this paper with free cocompletions under various colimit shapes. In formal category theory, as in enriched category theory, the appropriate data by which to parameterise a colimit shape is a
weight
. In enriched category theory, it is customary to define a weight for a colimit simply to be a presheaf
[
Kel82
]
(cf.
??
). However, it has long been observed that it is more flexible to define a weight to be an arbitrary distributor
[
SW78
]
; in particular, this permits a single notion of weight for both limits and colimits. In maximum generality, for settings in which composites of distributors may not exist (for instance, if we are concerned with categories that are not necessarily small), it is most appropriate to consider
chains
of distributors
[
Kou24
, §1.11]
.

Definition 2.12
.

A
weight
in a virtual double category is a chain of loose-cells.

\underbrace{X_{0}{\mathrel{\to}^{p_{1}}}X_{1}{\mathrel{\to}^{p_{2}}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}^{p_{m}}}X_{m}}_{\vec{p}}

We write
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon X_{n}{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}X_{0}
or simply
\vec{p}\colon X_{n}{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}X_{0}
for this situation.
A weight is
unary
if
m=1
, i.e. it comprises a single loose-cell.

Note that, in contrast to classical definitions of weight in enriched category theory
[
Kel82
,
AK88
,
KS05
]
, we do not impose any smallness assumptions in the definition of a weight. In practice, it is often useful to talk about certain large colimits (e.g. adjoints, or large cointersections of epimorphisms
[
KK81
]
), and most of the properties of colimits we will consider are independent of size concerns.

The universal properties of weighted limits and weighted colimits in a virtual equipment are expressed in terms of right
extensions
and
lifts
respectively
[
Woo82
]
. In the following, we generalise the notions of
right lift
and
right extension
from
[
AM24
,
RV22
]
to permit arbitrary (rather than unary) weights (cf.
[
Kou24
, §1]
). We note that, for lifts and extensions in an arbitrary virtual double category, a stronger universal property involving tight-cells would be necessary, but in a virtual equipment this simpler definition suffices (cf.
[
Par24
, §7]
).

Definition 2.13
.

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight and let
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell.
A loose-cell
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Y
, equipped with a 2-cell
\varpi\colon p_{1},\ldots,p_{m},q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}\Rightarrow q
, is the
right lift
of
q
through
p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}
when every 2-cell as on the left below factors uniquely as a diagram of the form on the right below (where
n\geq 0
). We call
\varpi
the
counit
of the right lift.

Definition 2.14

(label=lifting)
.

A weight
\vec{p}\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
is
lifting
if all right lifts through
\vec{p}
exist, i.e. if, for every loose-cell
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
, a right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Y
exists.

A right extension in a virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
is, by definition, a right lift in
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
. We spell out the definition for convenience.

Definition 2.15
.

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
be a weight and let
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell. A loose-cell
\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z
equipped with a 2-cell
\varpi\colon\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q,p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\Rightarrow q
is the
right extension
of
q
along
p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}

Definition 2.16

(label=extending)
.

A weight
\vec{p}\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
is
extending
if all right extensions along
\vec{p}
exist, i.e. if, for every loose-cell
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
, a right extension
\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z
exists.

In the presence of left- and right-composites, lifts through, and extensions along, arbitrary weights are no more general than lifts through, and extensions along, unary weights.

Lemma 2.17
.

Let
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell.

(2.17.(1))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight. If the left-composite
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}
exists (
1\leq i\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i},p_{i+1},\ldots,p_{m})

(2.17.(2))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
be a weight. If the right-composite
p_{i}\mathbin{{\odot}_{R}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{R}}p_{m}
exists (
1\leq i\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q\cong(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i-1},p_{i}\mathbin{{\odot}_{R}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{R}}p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q

Proof.

We focus on (1), since (2) follows by duality. Suppose that
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})
exists. By the universal property of
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}
, the counit
\varpi
factors uniquely through a 2-cell
\check{\varpi}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\check{\varpi}}

Now, suppose we are given a 2-cell
\phi
as follows, which we may precompose by the left-opcartesian 2-cell defining
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

By the universal property of the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})
, this factors uniquely through
\varpi
as
\lambda\phi
. Finally, pasting the left-opcartesian 2-cell on top of the following 2-cell exhibits the composite as equal to the 2-cell above, so that the following 2-cell is equal to
\phi
by the universal property of the left-opcartesian 2-cell.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{i+1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lambda\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\check{\varpi}}

Thus
\lambda\phi
exhibits
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})
as having the universal property of the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{i},p_{i+1},\ldots,p_{m})
. The converse follows by entirely analogous reasoning.
∎

In the presence of actual loose-composites, we have the following stronger statement.

Lemma 2.18
.

(2.18.(1))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight. If the loose-composite
{p_{i}\odot\cdots\odot p_{j}}
exists (
0\leq i\leq j\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i}\odot\cdots\odot p_{j},\ldots,p_{m})

(2.18.(2))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
be a weight. If the loose-composite
{p_{i}\odot\cdots\odot p_{j}}
exists (
0\leq i\leq j\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q\cong(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i}\odot\cdots\odot p_{j},\ldots,p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q

Proof.

The reasoning is analogous to that of
??
, making use of the stronger universal property of a loose-composite.
∎

Iterated lifts may be reduced to individual lifts, and similarly for extensions.

Lemma 2.19
.

Let
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell.

(2.19.(1))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight. If the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i})
exists (
0\leq i\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i})\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{i+1},\ldots,p_{m})\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})

(2.19.(2))

Let
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
be a weight. If the right extension
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i})
exists (
0\leq i\leq m
), then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

(p_{1},\ldots,p_{i})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}(p_{i+1},\ldots,p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q\cong(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q

Proof.

The reasoning in (1) follows as in
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.5]
, the universal properties of the loose-cells in question evidently being equivalent. (2) is dual.
∎

If all right lifts exist, then every left-composite is furthermore a composite. While, in practice, the existence of
all
right lifts or extensions tends to be too strong an assumption, the following lemma provides a useful special case of this fact.

Lemma 2.20
.

Suppose we are given a chain of loose-morphisms, for which the left-composites
q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}
and
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{l}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m})
exist.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}

If the weight
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{l})
is lifting, then the following 2-cell is left-opcartesian.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{l}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}

Proof.

Suppose we are given a 2-cell as follows.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

Invoking in turn the universal properties of the right lift
s\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{l})
, the left-composite
q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}
, and the left-composite
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{l}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m})
, the 2-cell
\phi
is equal to the following composite, in which
\psi
is the factorisation of
((1_{p_{1}},\ldots,1_{p_{l}},\widecheck{\lambda\phi})\mathbin{;}\varpi)
through the latter left-opcartesian 2-cell, establishing the existence aspect of the required universal property.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdot}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{l}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}_{l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}

Uniqueness follows from the conjunction of the uniqueness aspects of the universal properties of the respective left-composite, left-composite, and right lift.
∎

The proofs of the following lemmas, which establish the interaction between right lifts, right extensions, and restrictions, are exactly as their correspondents in
[
AM24
, §3]
and are omitted.

Lemma 2.21

(cf.
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.4]
)
.

Let
\vec{p}=p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
and
\vec{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{n})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be weights and
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell.
Suppose that the right extension
\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q
and right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{r}
exist. Then, if either side of the following exists, so does the other, in which case they are isomorphic.

(\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{r}\cong\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{r})

Lemma 2.22

(cf.
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.6]
)
.

Let
q\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell and
y\colon Y^{\prime}\to Y
be a tight-cell.

(2.22.(1))

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight and
x\colon X^{\prime}\to X
be a tight-cell. If the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}
exists, then
(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p})(y,x)\cong q(1,x)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}(1,y))
.

(2.22.(2))

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Y
be a weight and
z\colon Z^{\prime}\to Z
be a tight-cell. If the right extension
\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q
exists, then
(\vec{p}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q)(z,y)\cong(p_{1}(y,1),\ldots,p_{m}\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q(z,1))
.
∎

2.3.
Limits and colimits

We are now ready to introduce weighted limits and weighted colimits in virtual equipments. The following definitions generalise the notions in
[
AM24
, Definitions 3.8 & 3.9]
to permit arbitrary (rather than unary) weights. Consequently, they coincide with the
left Kan extensions
and
right Kan extensions
of
[
Kou24
, Definition 1.9 & Remark 1.6]
(though
[
Kou24
]
defines these in a virtual double category more generally, without assuming the existence of companions or conjoints).

Definition 2.23
.

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight and
f\colon Z\to X
be a tight-cell. A
\vec{p}
-weighted cocone
(or simply
\vec{p}
-cocone
) for
f
is a pair
(c,\gamma)
of a tight-cell
c\colon Y\to X
and a 2-cell
\gamma\colon p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\Rightarrow X(f,c)
.

preserves a colimit if and only if its conjoint

respects the colimit.

An
absolute colimit
is a colimit that is preserved by any functor or, equivalently, a colimit that is preserved by the presheaf embedding
[
Par69
]
. We may generalise the latter description by parameterising it with respect to a distributor.

For a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
, a colimit in
E
is
j
-absolute
if it is
E(j,1)
-absolute
[
AM24
, Definition 3.21]
. A colimit in
E
is
absolute
if it is
1_{E}
-absolute.

Note that, when we talk of
preservation of absolute colimits
, we simply mean that absolute colimits are sent to (not necessarily absolute) colimits. The following lemma provides a useful method to recognise absolute colimits, and generalises
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.23]
from tight-cells to loose-cells (upon taking
j
to be corepresentable), for which we require the notion of
density
for a loose-cell.

Definition 2.29

(
[
AM25a
, Definition 6.8]
)
.

A loose-cell
p\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}A
is
dense
when the identity 2-cell
1_{p}\colon p\Rightarrow p
exhibits
B(1,1)\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}B
as the right lift
p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
. A tight-cell is
dense
if its conjoint is.

Lemma 2.30
.

Let
\vec{p}\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z

In addition to considering the preservation of colimits, we may consider their reflection.

Definition 2.33
.

Let
\vec{p}\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight, and let
f\colon Z\to W
and
g\colon W\to X
be tight-cells. We say that
g

reflects
\vec{p}
-colimits of
f
if a
\vec{p}
-cocone
(c,\gamma)
for
f
is colimiting only if the
\vec{p}
-cocone
((c\mathbin{;}g),(\gamma\mathbin{;}g))
for
(f\mathbin{;}g)
is colimiting.

Example 2.34
.

A tight-cell
(non-strictly) creates
weighted colimits, in the sense of
[
AM25
, Definition 3.2
′
]
, if and only if it preserves and reflects weighted colimits.

In particular, all limits and colimits are reflected by fully faithful tight-cells.

Definition 2.35

(
[
AM24
, Corollary 3.28]
)
.

A tight-cell
f\colon A\to B
is
fully faithful
if
A(1,1)\cong B(f,f)
.

Fully faithful tight-cells reflect weighted limits and colimits.

Absoluteness allows us to characterise when weighted colimits are fully faithful (we shall not use this result here, but record it as a useful lemma).

Lemma 2.37

(label=ff-weighted-colimit)
.

Let
p\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z

2.4.
Adjunctions and reflections

Some of the most important properties concerning limits and colimits regard their interaction with adjunctions and, more generally, relative adjunctions. Relative adjunctions were studied in detail in
[
AM24
, §5]
; we recall some of the basic properties that will be relevant to us here.

Definition 2.38

(
[
AM24
, Definition 5.1]
)
.

A
relative adjunction
in a virtual equipment comprises the following data.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

(2.38.(1))

A tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
, the
root
.

(2.38.(2))

A tight-cell
\ell\colon A\to C
, the
left (relative) adjoint
.

(2.38.(3))

A tight-cell
r\colon C\to E
, the
right (relative) adjoint
.

(2.38.(4))

An isomorphism
C(\ell,1)\cong E(j,r)
.

In this situation, we write
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
. An
adjunction
is a relative adjunction whose root is the identity, in which case we write
\ell\dashv r
.

The proof of the following proposition is exactly as its correspondents in
[
AM24
, §3]
(where only unary weights were considered) and is omitted.

Proposition 2.39
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell.

(2.39.(1))

If
\ell\colon A\to C
is a left
j
-adjoint, then
\ell
preserves every colimit that
j
preserves
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.11]
.

(2.39.(2))

If
j
is dense and
r\colon C\to E
is a right
j
-adjoint, then
r
preserves limits
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.12]
.
∎

Corollary 2.40
.

Every dense and fully faithful tight-cell creates weighted limits.

Proof.

Let
f\colon A\to B
be a dense and fully faithful tight-cell. Fully faithful tight-cells reflect weighted limits by
??
. Furthermore,
1\mathrel{\dashv_{f}}f
since
f
is fully faithful. Hence, it preserves weighted limits since it is dense, by
??
.
∎

A particular class of adjunctions in which we shall be interested are the
reflections
, which are those with invertible counit; equivalently, they are those adjunctions for which the right adjoint is fully faithful in the sense of
??
. Our main interest in reflections herein is the following lemma, which demonstrates that reflective subobjects inherit colimits.

.

The following lemma, which establishes the good behaviour of right lifts through fully faithful tight-cells, generalises

AM24
, Lemma 3.29]
from tight-cells to loose-cells (upon taking

Lemma 2.42
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell. If
j
is fully faithful, then, for every loose-cell
p\colon X\to A
for which the right lift
(p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,1),\varpi)
exists, the 2-cell
\varpi\colon(p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,1))(j,1)\Rightarrow p
is invertible.

Proof.

The 2-cell
\varpi
is equal to the composite of the following isomorphisms,

p\cong p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}A(1,1)\cong p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,j)\cong(p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,1))(j,1)

using full faithfulness of
j
and
??
.
∎

2.5.
Pointwise extensions

A particularly important class of limits and colimits are extensions of one tight-cell along another: these correspond to the
pointwise
extensions in enriched category theory
[
AM24
, §3.3]
.

Definition 2.43
.

Let
j\colon Z\to Y
and
f\colon Z\to X
be tight-cells. A
(pointwise) left extension

j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f\colon Y\to X
of
f
along
j
is a
Y(j,1)
-weighted colimit of
f
.

A (pointwise) right extension in
\mathbb{X}
is a left extension in
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
.

Definition 2.44
.

Let
j\colon Z\to Y
and
f\colon Z\to X
be tight-cells. A
(pointwise) right extension

j\mathbin{{\blacktriangleright}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\cdot}}}f\colon Y\to X
of
f
along
j
is a
Y(1,j)
-weighted limit of
f
.

As in
[
AM24
, §3]
, we shall speak simply of
left
and
right extensions
, the notion of right extensions of loose-cells (
??
) being distinguished from right extensions of tight-cells (
??
) by the context. In any case, the two concepts are closely related: given tight-cells
j\colon Z\to Y
and
f\colon Z\to X
, the defining property of the right extension of tight-cells is
X(1,j\mathbin{{\blacktriangleright}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\cdot}}}f)\cong Y(1,j)\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}X(1,f)
.

We shall require a few properties of left extensions. The following lemma is handy for composing left extensions.

Lemma 2.45
.

Let
j
,
f
and
g
be tight-cells. Suppose that
j
is fully faithful, that the left extensions
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
and
j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g
exist, and that the latter preserves the former. Then
(f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j)\mathbin{;}(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g)\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g
.

Proof.

Using the preservation assumption, together with
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.29]
, we have the following.

(f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j)\mathbin{;}(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g)\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}(j\mathbin{;}(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g))\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}g\qed

The following lemma characterises when left extensions witness equivalences.

Lemma 2.46
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
and
f\colon A\to B
be tight-cells for which the left extensions
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j\colon B\to E
and
j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f\colon E\to B
exist and are adjoint:
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j\dashv j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f
.

(2.46.(1))

The adjunction is coreflective if
j
is fully faithful,
f
is dense, and
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
is
j
-absolute.

(2.46.(2))

The adjunction is reflective if
f
is fully faithful and
j
is dense.

In particular, the adjunction is an equivalence if both
f
and
j
are dense and fully faithful, and
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
is
j
-absolute.

Proof.

(1) Since
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
is
j
-absolute by assumption, it is preserved by
j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f
by
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.22]
, hence
??
implies
(f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j)\mathbin{;}(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f)\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f\cong 1
, exhibiting coreflectivity. (2) Since
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
is a left adjoint, it preserves all left extensions, so
??
implies
(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f)\mathbin{;}(f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j)\cong j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j\cong 1
.
∎

2.6.
Adjoints as absolute lifts

We now have almost everything we need to begin our study of presheaf constructions and cocompletions. Before doing so, we explain the relation between adjunctions and extensions, which will be useful in studying adjointness properties for cocomplete objects.

Definition 2.47

(
[
AM24
, Definition 2.18]
)
.

A
loose-adjunction
in a virtual double category comprises the following data.

(2.47.(1))

Loose-cells
\ell\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}C
and
r\colon C{\mathrel{\to}}A
.

(2.47.(2))

A loose-identity for
A
and a loose-composite
r\odot\ell\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}A
.

(2.47.(3))

2-cells
\eta\colon\Rightarrow r\odot\ell
and
\varepsilon\colon\ell,r\Rightarrow C(1,1)

These data must satisfy the evident triangle identities. We denote this situation by
\ell\dashv r
.

Example 2.48

(
[
AM24
, Lemma 2.19]
)
.

Let
f\colon A\to C
be a tight-cell in a virtual equipment. Then
C(1,f)\dashv C(f,1)
. The unit is denoted
\mathbin{\smallfrown_{f}}\colon{}\Rightarrow C(f,f)
and the counit
\mathbin{\smallsmile_{f}}\colon C(1,f),C(f,1)\Rightarrow A(1,1)
.

The following observation is classical for 2-categories
[
SW78
, Proposition 2]
, but requires a little more care in the situation in which composites may not exist.

Proposition 2.49
.

Let
\ell\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}A
and
r\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}B
be loose-cells admitting a loose-composite
{r\odot\ell\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}B}
and let
\varepsilon\colon\ell,r\Rightarrow A(1,1)
be a 2-cell. The following are equivalent.

(2.49.(1))

The 2-cell
\varepsilon
exhibits the counit of a loose-adjunction
\ell\dashv r
.

(2.49.(2))

For any loose-cell
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
for which the loose-composite
r\odot p
exists, the 2-cell below exhibits the counit of a right lift
r\odot p\cong p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\ell
.

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{opcart}}

The 2-cell

(1

, the universal property of the right lift
p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\ell
follows by transposition, i.e. pasting with the unit
\eta\colon{}\Rightarrow r\odot\ell
, uniqueness of the factorisation following from the triangle identities.

(2
\implies
3) The composite
A(1,1)\odot p
exists trivially, while the composite
r\odot\ell
exists by assumption.

(3
\implies
1) Given the specified right lifts, we define a unit

by applying the universal property of
\ell\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\ell
to the identity
1_{\ell}\colon\ell\Rightarrow\ell
; one triangle identity then follows immediately from the universal property.

As a consequence, we obtain the following ‘adjoint tight-cell theorem’.

Corollary 2.50

(cf.
[
SW78
,
Woo82
]
)
.

Let
f\colon A\to B
be a tight-cell. The following conditions are equivalent.

(2.50.(1))

f
admits a right adjoint.

(2.50.(2))

The left extension
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{A}\colon B\to A
exists and is absolute.

(2.50.(3))

The left extension
f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{A}\colon B\to A
exists and is preserved by
f
.

In this case, the unit of the left extension exhibits the unit of the adjunction
f\dashv f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{A}
.

Proof.

(1
\iff
2) follows from
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.10]
. For (1
\iff
3), observe that,
for each tight-cell
u\colon B\to A
, the loose-composite
A(u,1)\odot B(f,1)\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}B
is exhibited by
B(uf,1)
. By
??
, a 2-cell
B(1,fu)\Rightarrow B(1,1)
therefore exhibits the counit of a loose-adjunction
B(f,1)\dashv A(u,1)
if and only if it exhibits the counit of a right lift
A(u,1)\cong A(1,1)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}B(f,1)
, hence a left extension
u\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{A}
, and this is preserved by
f
. In particular,
B(f,1)\dashv A(u,1)
if and only if
f\dashv u
, from which the result follows.
∎

3.
Presheaves in a virtual equipment

A
presheaf object
in a virtual equipment axiomatises the structure of a category of presheaves
[
AM25a
, §7.1]
. Its universal property expresses the bijection discussed in the
??
, between loose-cells
A{\mathrel{\to}}B
and tight-cells
A\to\mathcal{P}B
. In particular, the identity
1_{\mathcal{P}A}\colon\mathcal{P}A\to\mathcal{P}A
induces a loose-cell
\pi_{A}\colon\mathcal{P}A{\mathrel{\to}}A
, which we require to be dense in the sense of
??
. (This distinguishes presheaf objects from
power objects

[
Lam22
, §11]
, in which
\pi_{A}
is not required to be dense; see
[
AM25a
, Remark 7.4]
for a discussion of related concepts.) We may refine the notion of presheaf object by parameterising it by a class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of loose-cells, requiring that the projection
\pi_{A}
witnesses a bijection between loose-cells
A{\mathrel{\to}}B
in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
and tight-cells from
A
into the
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object on
B
.

Remark 3.1

(A comment on notation)
.

Before we present the definition, it is necesssary to clarify a distinction between classical enriched category theory and formal category theory, which was mentioned in passing in
??
. For the theory of categories enriched in a monoidal category, it is typical to consider two notions of weight, depending on whether one is considering limits or colimits
[
Kel82
]
: colimits are weighted by presheaves (equivalently distributors from the trivial
\mathbf{V}
-category), while limits are weighted by copresheaves (equivalently distributors to the trivial
\mathbf{V}
-category). This means that it is often reasonable to use the same notation for both colimit notions and limit notions (e.g. free completions under a class of weights and free cocompletions under a class of weights), since these notions will be disambiguated by whether one is considering a class of weights for colimits, or a class of weights for limits. (Strictly speaking, when enriching in a braided monoidal category, presheaves on
{\mathbf{A}}
are in bijection with copresheaves on
{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}
, which means that the two notions of weight do coincide. However, the two notions are distinguished notationally in practice via the presence or absence of
op
.) In the setting of formal category theory, the appropriate notion of weight (
??
) is entirely symmetric, and parameterises both limits and colimits. We must therefore take care in our notation to be clear about whether we are talking about limit notions or colimit notions. We decorate operations with
\hat{\ }
and
\check{\ }
to denote colimit notions and limit notions respectively, which aligns with the typical convention in enriched category theory to denote the category of presheaves by
\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}
and the category of copresheaves by
\widecheck{{\mathbf{A}}}
.

Henceforth, we shall work in the setting of an ambient strict virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
(see
??
and the following discussion).

Definition 3.2
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a class of loose-cells in
\mathbb{X}
and let
A
be an object. A
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object
for
A
comprises an object
{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]
and a dense loose-cell
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\colon{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]{\mathrel{\to}}A
, such that

(3.2.(1))

for every loose-cell
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
, there is a unique tight-cell
\arch{p}\colon X\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]
satisfying
p=\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}(1,\arch{p})
;

(3.2.(2))

for every tight-cell
f\colon X\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]
, the restriction
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}(1,f)\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
.

Typically, when there is no risk of confusion, we will denote
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}
simply by
\pi_{A}
.

Note in particular that:

•

for each
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object,
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}=\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}(1,1)
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
, and
\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{640377}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{640377}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{543004}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{515710}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}=1_{{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]}
;

•

Example 3.4
.

Denote by

Remark 3.5

(label=P-presheaf-object-is-stronger-than-presheaf-object-in-sub-equipment)
.

Given a class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of loose-cells in the virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
, closed under restrictions and loose-identities, we can consider the full sub-virtual equipment spanned by loose-cells in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
. A
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object in
\mathbb{X}
is, in particular, a presheaf object in the sub-virtual equipment (in the sense of
??
). However the converse is not necessarily true: density of
\pi_{A}\colon{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]{\mathrel{\to}}A
in
\mathbb{X}
is typically a stronger condition than density in the sub-virtual equipment, as it refers to arbitrary loose-cells in
\mathbb{X}
. It therefore does not seem sufficient to study
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf constructions generally merely by considering presheaf constructions in sub-virtual equipments (or sub-augmented virtual equipments, cf.
??
).

Strictly speaking, the class of loose-cells in
??
is underconstrained, as the universal property of a presheaf object on an object
A
only involves loose-cells with codomain
A
. Therefore, we may always restrict a class of loose-cells to the loose-cells with a fixed codomain, without changing the notion of presheaf object.

Lemma 3.6
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a class of loose-cells and let
A
be an object. Denote by
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}|_{{}{\mathrel{\to}}A}
the subclass of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
spanned by loose-cells with codomain

. Then
A
admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object if and only if it admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}|_{{}{\mathrel{\to}}A}
-presheaf object.

Proof.

The universal property of
??
only involves loose-cells with codomain
A
.
∎

However, in practice, we typically wish to consider larger classes of weights than the one minimally determined by
??
, as we are often interested in comparing
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf objects on different objects.

Remark 3.7
.

Note that, if a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object exists, then necessarily

\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}|_{{}{\mathrel{\to}}A}=\{\ \pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}(1,f)\mid f\colon\cdot\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]\ \}

(where
\cdot
denotes an arbitrary object). However, typically we wish to start with a class of loose-cells, and then form a presheaf object with respect to that class, rather than conversely. We will give conditions in
??
under which a given loose-cell
\pi\colon P{\mathrel{\to}}A
exhibits a presheaf object for the canonically associated class of loose-cells
\{\ \pi(1,f)\mid f\colon\cdot\to E\ \}
.

It is worth highlighting that
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf objects are unique up to isomorphism, rather than up to equivalence. While this tends to be convenient in practice, it does mean that the relationship between the class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
and the notion of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object is rather strict. To illustrate this point, let us consider a natural operation on a class of loose-cells: closing under isomorphism.

Definition 3.8
.

The
repletion

\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{{\cong}}
of a class of loose-cells
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
in a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
is the closure of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
under (globularly) isomorphic loose-cells. A class of loose-cells is
replete
if it is equal to its repletion, i.e.
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}=\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{{\cong}}
.

While the classes
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
and
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{{\cong}}
may seem ‘essentially the same’, a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object exhibits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{{\cong}}
-presheaf object only if
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
is replete.

Lemma 3.9
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
and
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
be classes of loose-cells and let
A
be an object. Suppose that a loose-cell
\pi_{A}\colon P{\mathrel{\to}}A
exhibits both a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
- and a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
-presheaf object for
A
. Then
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}|_{{}{\mathrel{\to}}A}=\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}|_{{}{\mathrel{\to}}A}
.

Proof.

Let
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
be a tight-cell in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
. Then
p=\pi_{A}(1,\arch{p})
by (
3.2.(1)
) for a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
-presheaf object, and hence
p\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
by (
3.2.(2)
) for a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object. The converse is symmetric.
∎

We now establish some basic properties of presheaf objects. One of the most important properties is that the homs of presheaf objects exhibit right lifts.

Generally speaking, a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object may not be ‘closed under representables’, in that we may not have a tight-cell
A\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]
. However, we shall primarily be interested in situations where we have such an embedding, for which we introduce the following definition.

Definition 3.17
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a class of loose-cells. An object
A
is
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-admissible
if it admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object, and
1_{A}\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{{\cong}}
.
In this case, we denote by

{\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A}\cong\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{1558308}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\displaystyle A(1,1)\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{1558308}{254863}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\textstyle A(1,1)\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{1267037}{204801}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptstyle A(1,1)\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern 0.80002pt$\hss\resizebox{1105389}{177495}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\hss\scriptscriptstyle A(1,1)\hss$\crcr}}}\limits}\colon A\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]

the
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf embedding of
A
, which is the essentially unique tight-cell satisfying
A(1,1)\cong\pi_{A}(1,{\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A})
.

\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-embeddings are the formal analogues of Yoneda embeddings, and are well behaved in the ways one would expect.

Lemma 3.18
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a class of loose-cells and let
A
be a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-admissible object.

(3.18.(1))

There is an isomorphism
{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]({\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A},1)\cong\pi_{A}
(cf.
[
AM25a
, Lemma 7.9]
).

(3.18.(2))

{\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A}
is dense and fully faithful.

(3.18.(3))

{\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A}
creates weighted limits (cf.
[
Shu13
, Theorem 10.28]
).

(3.18.(4))

For each weight
p\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
, the tight-cell
\arch{p}\colon X\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]
exhibits the
{\hat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}_{A}

\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-2.5pt}{-2.32639pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

Corollary 3.19
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}\subseteq\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
be classes of loose-cells and let

be a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-admissible and
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}^{\prime}
-admissible object. The induced tight-cell

(

) commutes with the presheaf embeddings up to isomorphism.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{A}]}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathchoice{\mathop{\vbox{\kern 0.67557pt$\scriptstyle\hss\resizebox{464065}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\scriptstyle\hss\displaystyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\kern 0.67557pt$\scriptstyle\hss\resizebox{464065}{124882}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\scriptstyle\hss\textstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\kern 0.67557pt$\scriptstyle\hss\resizebox{310281}{87418}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\scriptstyle\hss\scriptstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}\limits}{\mathop{\vbox{\kern 0.67557pt$\scriptstyle\hss\resizebox{268441}{62441}{\rotatebox[origin]{-90.0}{(}}\hss$\crcr\cr$\scriptstyle\hss\scriptscriptstyle\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}\hss$\crcr}}\limits}}

Proof.

The properties of presheaf objects established above will be sufficient for our study of free cocompletions, which is our concern here. In a sequel, we will study presheaf objects further in relation to
admissibility
and
realisability
, which is the study of abstract nerve constructions
[
SW78
,
BF99
]
.

4.
Atomicity

In the study of
\Phi
-cocompletions, an important concept is the notion of
\Phi
-atomicity
, which extends the concept of a
\Phi
-atom in a category
{\mathbf{A}}
, viz. an object
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
for which
{\mathbf{A}}(a,{-})\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}
preserves
\Phi
-colimits
[
KS05
, §4]
. We generalise this notion from objects in a category to loose-cells in a virtual equipment.

Definition 4.1
.

Let
\vec{p}\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a weight. A loose-cell
j\colon E{\mathrel{\to}}A
is a
\vec{p}
-atom
when
E
admits
\vec{p}
-weighted colimits and these colimits are
j
-absolute. Given a class of weights
\Phi
, we say that
j
is a
\Phi
-atom
if it is a
\vec{p}
-atom for each weight
\vec{p}\in\Phi
. A tight-cell is a
\vec{p}
-atom
, respectively
\Phi
-atom
, if its conjoint is.

Example 4.2
.

A functor
f\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{B}}
is a
\Phi
-atom if and only if
{\mathbf{B}}
is
\Phi
-cocomplete and the nerve functor
{\mathbf{B}}(f({-}_{2}),{-}_{1})\colon{\mathbf{B}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
is
\Phi
-cocontinuous
[
AM24
, Lemma 8.10]
. Since colimits in
{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
are computed pointwise, this equivalently says that, for each
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
, the functor
{\mathbf{B}}(f(a),{-})\colon{\mathbf{B}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}
is
\Phi
-cocontinuous, i.e. each object
f(a)
is a
\Phi
-atom in the classical sense. In particular, an object
b\in|{\mathbf{B}}|
is a
\Phi
-atom in the classical sense if and only if the corresponding functor
b\colon\mathbf{1}\to{\mathbf{B}}
is a
\Phi
-atom in the sense of
??
.

Consider
\Delta
a class of categories, which induces a class
\Phi
of weights by
\Phi\mathrel{:=}\{*\colon\mathbf{1}{\mathrel{\to}}\mathbf{J}\mid\mathbf{J}\in\Delta\}
, where
*
denotes the terminal presheaf.

(4.2.(1))

When
\Delta=\{\text{small discrete categories}\}
, the
\Phi
-atoms are called
abstractly exclusively unary

[
Bun66
]
,
Z-objects

[
Hof73
]
,
coprime

[
Bör89
]
, or
connected

[
EE78
]
.

(4.2.(2))

When
\Delta=\{\text{sifted categories}\}
, the
\Phi
-atoms are called
strongly finitely presentable

[
AR01
]
or
perfectly presentable

[
ARV10
]
.

(4.2.(3))

When
\Delta=\{\text{filtered categories}\}
, the
\Phi
-atoms are called
finitely presentable

[
GU71
]
or
compact

[
Lur03
]
.

(4.2.(4))

When
\Delta=\{\text{$\kappa$-filtered categories}\}
, for a regular cardinal
\kappa
, the
\Phi
-atoms are called
\kappa
-presentable

[
GU71
]
or
\kappa
-compact

[
Lur03
]
.

(4.2.(5))

When
\Delta=\{\text{small categories}\}
, the
\Phi

Lemma 4.3
.

Let

be a dense tight-cell and let

\ell

Remark 4.9
.

Density of a loose-cell
j\colon E{\mathrel{\to}}A
implies that it is ‘essentially monic’, i.e. given
f,f^{\prime}\colon X\to E
, if
j(1,f)\cong j(1,f^{\prime})
then
f\cong f^{\prime}
. The monicity condition in
??
is necessary because our presheaf objects are unique up to isomorphism, rather than equivalence.

The previous proposition motivates the following definition, which essentially characterises presheaf objects with respect to classes of weights that are particularly well behaved; the terminology follows
[
ACU15
, §4]
.

Definition 4.10
.

A tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
is
well-behaved
if the following conditions hold.

(4.10.(1))

j
is fully faithful.

(4.10.(2))

j
is dense.

(4.10.(3))

j
is an
E(j,1)
-atom, i.e. left extensions of tight-cells
A\to E
along
j
exist and are
j
-absolute.

We shall further study this property in
??
.

5.
Rank

Along with atomicity, a further important concept in the study of
\Phi
-cocompletions is the notion of
rank
with respect to a tight-cell, which extends the concept of the
accessibility rank
of a functor. Classically, a functor is said to have
rank

\kappa
, for a regular cardinal
\kappa
, if it preserves
\kappa
-filtered colimits (i.e. if it is
\kappa
-accessible
, a.k.a.
finitary
when
\kappa=\aleph_{0}
). The rank of a functor intuitively captures the ‘size’ of a functor: a functor with rank may typically be recovered by specifying a functor out of a smaller subcategory, and left-extending along the subcategory inclusion. The following definitions are intended to capture this intuition.

Definition 5.1
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell.

(5.1.(1))

A tight-cell
f\colon E\to I
has
rank

j
if the left extension
j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}(j\mathbin{;}f)
exists, and the canonical 2-cell
j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}(j\mathbin{;}f)\Rightarrow f
is invertible.

(5.1.(2))

A loose-cell
p\colon I{\mathrel{\to}}E
has
rank

j
if the right lift
p(j,1)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,1)
exists, and the canonical 2-cell
p\Rightarrow p(j,1)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}E(j,1)
is invertible.

In particular, a tight-cell
f\colon E\to I
has rank
j
precisely when its conjoint
I(f,1)\colon I{\mathrel{\to}}E
does.

Example 5.2
.

The most common situation in which to consider rank is when the functor
j\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to{\mathbf{E}}
exhibits the cocompletion of a small category under a class of colimits. In this situation, the property of having rank
j
admits several equivalent formulations. Since we establish these equivalent characterisations in full generality in
??
, we shall only give a few illustrative examples here.

(5.2.(1))

Let
j\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{Ind}({\mathbf{A}})
denote the cocompletion of a small category
{\mathbf{A}}
under filtered colimits. A functor from
\mathbf{Ind}({\mathbf{B}})
is
finitary
precisely when it has rank
j
, which holds if and only if it preserves filtered colimits.

(5.2.(2))

Let
j\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{Sind}({\mathbf{A}})
denote the cocompletion of a small category
{\mathbf{A}}
under sifted colimits. A functor is
strongly finitary
precisely when it has rank
j
, which holds if and only if it preserves sifted colimits.

Example 5.3
.

Rank may be viewed as a generalisation of the concept of density: a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
is dense precisely when the identity
1_{E}
on its codomain has rank
j
.

The following proposition establishes a close connection between rank, the property of being a left extension, and preservation of absolute colimits.

6.
Cocompleteness and cocompletions in a virtual equipment

A
cocompletion
in a virtual equipment axiomatises the universal property of a free cocompletion of a category under a class of colimits. When considering free cocompletions in ordinary category theory, one typically asks that every functor
f\colon{\mathbf{A}}\to\mathbf{X}
into a category
\mathbf{X}
admitting a certain class
\Phi
of colimits may be extended to a functor
\tilde{f}\colon{\widehat{\Phi}}({\mathbf{A}})\to\mathbf{X}
from the free cocompletion, in an essentially unique way. While this universal property certainly plays a role in our treatment, it is important for us to observe that free cocompletions also admit a second universal property, which concerns distributors
p\colon\mathbf{X}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
satisfying an exactness property with respect to
\Phi
. The notion of cocompletion we consider, therefore, is stronger than the 2-categorical universal property that has been considered heretofore in the literature. As we will explain later, this stronger universal property allows us to establish desirable properties of free cocompletions that do not follow from the mere 2-categorical universal property: for instance, the embedding of any object into a cocompletion in our sense is fully faithful (
??
), whereas there are pathological examples of cocompletions in the 2-categorical sense for which this is not the case (
??
).

We shall start by introducing the appropriate notion of cocompleteness in our setting (
??
), before introducing and studying cocompletions (
??
).

6.1.
Cocompleteness

The notion of completeness of an object and the cocontinuity of a tight-cell with respect to a class of weights is straightforward, being formulated exactly as in enriched category theory. However, we shall also need a notion of
exactness
of a loose-cell with respect to a class of weights, which plays an analogous role to cocontinuity for tight-cells.

Definition 6.1
.

Let
\Phi
be a class of weights.

(6.1.(1))

A
\Phi
-colimit
is a
\vec{p}
-weighted colimit for some
\vec{p}\in\Phi
.

(6.1.(2))

An object
A
is
\Phi
-cocomplete
if, for every tight-cell
f\colon D\to A
and weight
\vec{p}\colon W{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}D
in
\Phi
, there exists a colimit
