.

(6.1.(3))

A tight-cell
g\colon A\to B
with
\Phi
-cocomplete domain is
\Phi
-cocontinuous
if it preserves every
\Phi
-colimit.

(6.1.(4))

A loose-cell
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
with
\Phi
-cocomplete codomain is
\Phi
-exact
if it respects every
\Phi
-colimit (in the sense of
??
).

In particular, a tight-cell
g\colon A\to B
with
\Phi
-cocomplete domain is
\Phi
-cocontinuous if and only if its conjoint
B(g,1)\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}A
is
\Phi
-exact.

6.2.
Saturation

In general, there may be many classes of weights whose notions of cocompleteness coincide: for instance, in the setting of ordinary categories, the existence of all small colimits may be reduced to many different bases, such as:

•

small coproducts and (reflexive) coequalisers;

•

an initial object and wide pushouts;

•

finite coproducts and sifted colimits;

•

finite colimits and filtered colimits,

and so on.
We introduce the following equivalence class on classes of weights to capture this relationship.

Definition 6.2

(label=colimit-equivalence)
.

Two classes of weights
\Phi
and
\Phi^{\prime}
are
colimit equivalent
, written
\Phi\mathrel{\hat{\approx}}\Phi^{\prime}
, if and only if
\Phi\mathrel{\hat{\lesssim}}\Phi^{\prime}
and
\Phi^{\prime}\mathrel{\hat{\lesssim}}\Phi
, where
\Phi\mathrel{\hat{\lesssim}}\Phi^{\prime}
holds if and only if

(6.2.(1))

every
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocomplete object is
\Phi
-cocomplete;

(6.2.(2))

every
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocontinuous tight-cell with
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocomplete domain is
\Phi
-cocontinuous;

(6.2.(3))

every
\Phi^{\prime}
-exact loose-cell with
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocomplete codomain is
\Phi
-exact.

Remark 6.3
.

Since a tight-cell
f\colon X\to Y
is
\Phi
-cocontinuous if and only if the loose-cell
Y(f,1)
is
\Phi
-exact, condition (2) above is redundant (and merely included for clarity).

The relation
\mathrel{\hat{\lesssim}}
defined in
??
forms a preorder on the collection of classes of weights, which is a quotient of the power class of weights (since
\Phi\subseteq\Phi^{\prime}
trivially implies
\Phi\mathrel{\hat{\lesssim}}\Phi^{\prime}
). We shall be interested in maximal elements, in the following sense.

Definition 6.4

(label=saturation)
.

Let
\Phi
be a class of weights. The
colimit saturation
of
\Phi

. However, in line with our approach to formal category theory
[
AM24
]
, we are concerned not with 2-categories, but with virtual equipments. Therefore, the appropriate notion of colimit saturation is one that also induces a correspondence between the appropriate notion of loose-cell between
\Phi
-cocomplete objects, which is precisely the notion of
\Phi
-exact loose-cell. Consequently, our notion of colimit saturation is, a priori, more constrained than the traditional definition, which omits condition (3) in
??
. Note also that, again in contrast to the traditional definition, we impose no size restrictions on our weights; and do not require in (2) that the
codomain
of a
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocontinuous tight-cell is
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocomplete.

6.3.
Cocompletions

We are ready to introduce the second concept central to the paper (following the
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf objects of

Definition 6.8
.

Let
\Phi
be a class of weights and let
A
be an object. A
\Phi
-cocompletion
of
A
comprises an object
{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)
and a tight-cell
{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\colon A\to{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)
such that the following conditions hold.

(6.8.(1))

{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)
is
\Phi
-cocomplete.

(6.8.(2))

For each tight-cell
f\colon A\to X
with
\Phi
-cocomplete codomain, the left extension
{{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f\colon{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)\to X}
exists, the unit
f\Rightarrow{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\mathbin{;}({\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f)
is invertible, and
{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}f
is the essentially unique
\Phi
-cocontinuous tight-cell
\tilde{f}\colon{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)\to X
such that
f\cong({\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\mathbin{;}\tilde{f})
.

(6.8.(3))

For each loose-cell
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}A
, the right lift
{p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1)\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)}
exists, the canonical 2-cell
(p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1))({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1)\Rightarrow p
is invertible, and
p\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1)
is the essentially unique
\Phi
-exact loose-cell
\tilde{p}\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)
such that
p\cong\tilde{p}({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1)
.

An object is
\Phi
-cocompletable
if it admits a
\Phi
-cocompletion.

In particular, for a
\Phi
-cocompletion
{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\colon A\to{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)
, the conjoint
{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)({\hat{\Phi}}_{A},1)\colon{\widehat{\Phi}}(A){\mathrel{\to}}A
is lifting (
??
).

.

Since a tight-cell between
\Phi
-cocomplete objects is
\Phi
-cocontinuous if and only if its conjoint is
\Phi
-exact, we may replace (2) in

with the following condition.

•

As indicated earlier, the notion of cocompletion is invariant under colimit equivalence.

Note that, as anticipated at the start of the section,
??

that free cocompletions of enriched categories do indeed satisfy this stronger universal property. This is a typical phenomenon in double category theory: for instance, algebra objects for monads in virtual equipments satisfy a stronger universal property than algebra objects for monads in 2-categories (see the discussion after
[

Lemma 6.11

Every
\Phi

{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}\colon A\to{\widehat{\Phi}}(A)

Proof.

By

Example 6.12
.

A given tight-cell may exhibit cocompletions for different classes of weights, which may not be colimit equivalent. An elementary example is the functor
1\colon\mathbf{1}\to{\mathbf{Set}}
picking out a singleton set, which exhibits the cocompletion of the terminal category under either (a) small coproducts; or (b) small colimits. However, for each cocompletion
j\colon A\to E
, there is a canonical class of weights for which
j
exhibits a cocompletion: namely, the (singleton) class of weights for left extensions along
j
.

\Phi

be a tight-cell exhibiting the

Proof.

Assuming each of the conditions of

for

are trivially verified.

The reader will note that the conditions imposed by

Proposition 6.21

{\hat{\Phi}}_{A}

Remark 6.22

Remark 6.23
.

[
Wal18
]
shows that every lax-idempotent pseudomonad on a 2-category induces a Yoneda structure on the same 2-category. Conceptually, this expresses that free cocompletions (in the 2-categorical sense, i.e. satisfying merely conditions (1 & 2) of

??
may be seen as an analogue of this result in the setting of virtual equipments.

Conversely, being well-behaved is sufficient to be a cocompletion under some class of weights, assuming the existence of enough right lifts.

Corollary 6.24
.

A tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
exhibits the

-cocompletion of

if and only if it is well-behaved and
E(j,1)
is lifting.

Proof.

We invoke
??
with
\Phi\mathrel{:=}\{E(j,1)\}
. If the cocompletion exists, then it is well-behaved by

and satisfies the existence of right lifts by condition (3). Conversely, given that

admits left extensions along

, so that (1) holds. (2) is trivial. The existence of right lifts in (3) is by assumption; these are automatically
\{E(j,1)\}
-exact when they exist by
??
. (4) is by definition of being well-behaved.
∎

In particular, using

6.5.
Adjointness theorems

Cocompletions satisfy a particularly convenient test for adjointness.

Proposition 6.29

(cf.
[
Kel82
, Theorem 5.33]
)
.

Let
\Phi
be a class of weights and let

be a dense tight-cell with
\Phi
-cocomplete codomain. A
\Phi
-cocontinuous tight-cell

admits a right adjoint if and only if the left extension
(fj)\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j
exists.

Proof.

We have
(fj)\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}(j\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}j)\cong f\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1
since
j
is dense, using
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.16]
. Furthermore, this left extension, being a
\Phi
-colimit, is preserved by
f
, from which the result follows by
??
.
∎

Example 6.31
.

Let
{\mathbf{E}}
be a cocomplete category with a small dense subcategory
{\mathbf{A}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{E}}
(for instance, any locally presentable category). Then every cocontinuous functor
{\mathbf{E}}\to\mathbf{X}
(where
\mathbf{X}
is not necessarily cocomplete) admits a right adjoint.

6.7.

,

-cocompletions (

]

Throughout the paper so far, we have focused on presheaf objects and cocompletions. The theory of

Definition
2.3
co
.

A loose-cell

is

when the identity 2-cell

exhibits
A(1,1)\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}A

if its companion is.

Definition
3
co
.

Let

(8.0.(1))

for every tight-cell

\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{A}(f,1)\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}X

.

Typically, when there is no risk of confusion, we will denote

9.
Cocompletions of enriched categories

To demonstrate the utility of the theory we have developed, we instantiate our main results in the context of virtual equipments of enriched categories, providing constructions of completions and cocompletions of enriched categories under classes of weights. Beyond merely justifying the applicability of our results, this fills a conspicuous gap in the literature: while such constructions are well known to exist in the setting of enrichment in particularly nice monoidal categories, it does not appear that the existence of these constructions has been demonstrated even for categories enriched in non-symmetric monoidal categories, let alone for categories enriched in bicategories, despite the importance of these settings. (We give a survey of completion results in the literature in
??
.)

9.1.
Categories enriched in virtual bicategories

In fact, we shall consider a setting slightly more general than that of enrichment in bicategories. It was observed by
[
Lei02
]
that it is natural to enrich categories not merely in monoidal categories, but in virtual double categories (enrichment in a monoidal category being recovered by considering a monoidal category to be a one-object virtual double category). Here, we shall be concerned with the special case of enrichment in normal virtual bicategories
5
5

5

The reason for considering enrichment merely in normal virtual bicategories, rather than in the most general setting, is that there are several subtleties arising in the theory of enrichment in virtual double categories that must be addressed before developing the corresponding formal category theory. In the interest of space, we defer such considerations to a future paper.
. Recall that a virtual double category is normal when it admits loose-identities (
??
).

Definition 9.1
.

A (
normal
)
virtual bicategory
is a (normal) virtual double category in which every tight-cell is an identity.

A normal virtual bicategory is thus a structure akin to a bicategory – in particular, possessing identity 1-cells – but without the ability to compose 1-cells, instead having multiary 2-cells
f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\Rightarrow g
.

Example 9.2
.

Every multicategory (and, in particular, every monoidal category)
{\mathbf{M}}
forms a virtual bicategory
\Sigma{\mathbf{M}}
with a single object, the loose-cells of
\Sigma{\mathbf{M}}
being the objects of
{\mathbf{M}}
, and the 2-cells of
\Sigma{\mathbf{M}}
being the multimorphisms of
{\mathbf{M}}
.

Since the concept of enrichment in virtual bicategories is not widely known, we recall the relevant definitions.

{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
q(f,g)\mathrel{:=}(a,b)\mapsto q(f(a),g(b))
.

Definition 9.10
.

If
{\mathbb{V}}
is a normal virtual bicategory, then, for every object
V\in{\mathbb{V}}
, there is a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
\star_{V}
having a single object of extent
V
, whose hom-morphism is the loose-identity on
V
.
To give a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
\star_{V}\to{\mathbf{A}}
is equivalently to choose a single object
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
of extent
V
.
Below, we will use this correspondence implicitly, writing
a
for both the object and the
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor.
Similarly,
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors
p\colon\star_{V}{\mathrel{\to}}\star_{V^{\prime}}
are in bijection with loose-cells
p\colon V{\mathrel{\to}}V^{\prime}
.

9.2.
Enriched presheaves

In light of
??
, to construct cocompletions, we are led to consider enriched categories of presheaves.

Definition 9.11

(label=presheaf)
.

A
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf

p
on a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
comprises an object
\underline{p}
of
{\mathbb{V}}
(the
extent
of
p
), together with a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
\star_{\underline{p}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
: explicitly, this comprises a morphism
p(a)\colon\underline{p}{\mathrel{\to}}\underline{a}
in
{\mathbb{V}}
for each object
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
; and a left-action of
{\mathbf{A}}
on
p
, i.e. a 2-cell
\circ_{a^{\prime},a}\colon{\mathbf{A}}(a^{\prime},a),p(a)\Rightarrow p(a^{\prime})
in
{\mathbb{V}}
for each pair of objects
a,a^{\prime}\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
, compatible with identities and composition in
{\mathbf{A}}
.
Dually, a
{\mathbb{V}}
-copresheaf

q
on
{\mathbf{A}}
comprises an object
\underline{q}
of
{\mathbb{V}}
, together with a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
{\mathbf{A}}{\mathrel{\to}}\star_{\underline{p}}
.

Since we define
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves in terms of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors, we can speak of a right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
of
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves
p,q
on
{\mathbf{A}}
.
Such a right lift is a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
\star_{\underline{q}}{\mathrel{\to}}\star_{\underline{p}}
or, equivalently, a loose-cell
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p\colon\underline{q}{\mathrel{\to}}\underline{p}
in
{\mathbb{V}}
.
These right lifts will provide the hom-morphisms of each
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf object.
When we take
{\mathbb{V}}=\Sigma\mathbf{V}
for a symmetric monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}
, a
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf on
{\mathbf{A}}
is equivalently a
\mathbf{V}
-functor
{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{V}
, and the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
is the hom-object
[{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathbf{V}](p,q)
of the
\mathbf{V}
-functor category
[{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathbf{V}]
, when the latter exists.
A more detailed discussion of these points can be found in
[
AM24
, Section 8.1]
, which uses the notation
\mathcal{P}{A}(p,q)
for a right lift of presheaves.

Right lifts of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors can be reduced to right lifts of
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves by the following lemma.

Lemma 9.12
.

Let
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\colon{\mathbf{A}}_{n}{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}_{0}
be a weight in
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
, with
n\geq 1
.

(9.12.(1))

Let
q\colon{\mathbf{B}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}_{0}
be a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor.
If it exists, the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}\colon{\mathbf{B}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}_{n}
satisfies

(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p})(a,b)\cong q(1,b)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\dots,p_{n-1},p_{n}(1,a))

for all
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}_{n}|
and
b\in|{\mathbf{B}}|
.
If the right-hand side exists for all
a
and
b
, then so does
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\vec{p}
(cf.
[
AM24
, Lemma 8.7]
).

(9.12.(2))

If it exists, the left-composite
(p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{n})\colon{\mathbf{A}}_{0}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}_{n}
satisfies

(p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{n})(1,a_{n})\cong p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{n-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(p_{n}(1,a_{n}))

for all
a_{n}\in|{\mathbf{A}}_{n}|
.
If the right-hand side exists for all
a_{n}
, then so does
p_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p_{n}
(cf.
[
AM24
, Lemma 8.7]
).

9.3.
Enriched presheaf objects

We turn now to the construction of presheaf objects (in the sense of
??
) in the virtual equipment
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
.
We cannot expect
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf objects to exist for every class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
; indeed an immediate consequence of the definition of presheaf object is that they can only exist when
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
is closed under restrictions
p(1,f)
(see
??
).
We thus restrict to classes of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors that are
induced
by a class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves in the following sense.

Definition 9.16

(label=presheaf-induced-class)
.

A class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors is
presheaf-induced
if a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
p\colon{\mathbf{B}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
if and only if, for each
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
, the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p(1,a)
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
.

For every class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves, there is a corresponding maximal presheaf-induced class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors.

Theorem 9.17

(label=enriched-presheaf-objects)
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a presheaf-induced class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf
{\mathbb{V}}
-category (
??
) if and only if the right lift
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
exists for all
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves
p,q\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
on
{\mathbf{A}}
. In this case,
{\mathbf{A}}
is furthermore
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-admissible (
??
) if and only if the repletion of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
contains the identity
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor on
{\mathbf{A}}
.

Proof.

First, the existence of the
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object implies the existence of the right lifts by
??
,
??
.

For the converse, assume the mentioned right lifts exist; we construct the
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object as follows.
The
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}]
has as objects the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves
p\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
on
{\mathbf{A}}
, and hom-cells
{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}](p,q)\mathrel{:=}q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
.
To exhibit this
{\mathbb{V}}
-category as a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object, we define the
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}\colon{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}]{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
by
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}(a,p)\mathrel{:=}p(a)
.
This
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor is dense:

{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}](p,q)=(\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}(1,q))\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}(1,q))=(\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}})(p,q)

To show that this is a presheaf object, we verify conditions (1) and (2) of
??
.

(9.17.(1))

Let
p\colon\mathbf{X}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
be a loose-cell in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
, i.e. a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor such that, for every
x\in|\mathbf{X}|
, the presheaf
p({-},x)
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
\arch{p}\colon\mathbf{X}\to{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}]
satisfies

p=\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}(1,\arch{p})
when the presheaves
p({-},x)
and
\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}({-},|\arch{p}|x)=|\arch{p}|x
are equal and
{\arch{p}}_{x,y}\colon\mathbb{X}(x,y)\Rightarrow{\widehat{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}](|\arch{p}|x,|\arch{p}|y)=p({-},y)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p({-},x)
is the unique factorisation of the action
\{p(a,x),\mathbf{X}(x,y)\Rightarrow p(a,y)\}_{a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|}

on
p

Existence and uniqueness of such a

(9.17.(2))

For every
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor

\pi^{\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}}_{\mathbf{A}}(1,f)\colon\mathbf{X}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}

The characterisation of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}

∎

A presheaf $p\colon{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}\to{\mathbf{Set}}$ on a (possibly large) category ${\mathbf{A}}$ is weakly multirepresentable\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{arkor2024adjoint}{}{}, \lx@sectionsign 1.1]} (a.k.a.{}\penalty\ \emph{proper}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{isbell1960adequate}{}{}, \lx@sectionsign 1]} or \emph{petty}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{freyd1968several}{}{}, \lx@sectionsign 1]}) when there exists an epimorphism $\sum_{i\in I}{\mathbf{A}}(1,a_{i})\twoheadrightarrow p$ in ${\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{A}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}$, for some small family $\{a_{i}\in|{\mathbf{A}}|\}_{i\in I}$ of objects of ${\mathbf{A}}$. In particular, every small presheaf, being expressible as a coequaliser of a coproduct of representable presheaves, is weakly multirepresentable.
\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{lack2023virtual}{}{}, Remark\penalty\ 4.39]} observe that the (locally small) category ${\widehat{\Phi}}[{{\mathbf{A}}}]$ of weakly multirepresentable presheaves satisfies the 2-categorical universal property of the completion of ${\mathbf{A}}$ under small colimits and (possibly large) cointersections of regular epimorphisms (cf.{}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{kelly1981large}{}{}]}).
We can apply our {\mbox{??}} to this case (although not {\mbox{??}}, since the weights in question have large domain), showing that the weakly multirepresentable presheaves satisfy our stronger definition of cocompletion. This demonstrates that our framework is an effective setting in which to study even large cocompletions (other such examples are given in {\mbox{??}}, {\mbox{??}}).
\par First, note that every weakly multirepresentable presheaf $p$ is lifting.
Indeed, $\sum_{i\in I}{\mathbf{A}}(1,a_{i})$ is lifting, with $q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}\sum_{i\in I}{\mathbf{A}}(1,a_{i})\cong\prod_{i\in I}(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\mathbf{A}}(1,a_{i}))\cong\prod_{i\in I}q(a_{i},1)$, so $q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p$ is given by a sub-copresheaf of $\prod_{i\in I}q(a_{i},1)$.
\par In any category, the cointersection of a $J$-indexed family of regular epimorphisms is equivalently the colimit of a diagram of shape ${\mathbf{W}}_{J}$, where the category ${\mathbf{W}}_{J}$ consists of an object $x$, and, for each $j\in J$, an object $w_{j}$ along with a parallel pair of morphisms $\ell_{j},r_{j}\colon w_{j}\to x$.
Thus, there is a class of weights $\Phi$ for small colimits and cointersections of regular epimorphisms, consisting of all presheaves on small categories, as well as the conical ${\mathbf{W}}_{J}$-indexed weights (i.e.{}{} presheaves $u_{J}\colon\star{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{W}}_{J}$, where $u_{J}$ sends every object of ${\mathbf{W}}_{J}$ to a singleton set).

9.5.
Small presheaves

One consequence of
??
is that the small cocompletion (where
\Phi=\{\text{ ${\mathbb{V}}$-presheaves on small ${\mathbb{V}}$-categories }\}
) of a general
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
exists under mild assumption on
{\mathbb{V}}
.
It is known that this cocompletion is given by the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of
small

{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves on
{\mathbf{A}}
(cf.
[
Kel82
, Section 5.6]
), though
??
does not directly give this characterisation.
More generally, for any subclass
\Phi^{\prime}\subseteq\Phi
, the
\Phi^{\prime}
-cocompletion is given by a sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves.
We have so far avoided any mention of small presheaves, but for completeness we discuss them here.

Definition 9.34

(label=small-presheaf)
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
be a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p
on
{\mathbf{A}}
is
small
when there exists a full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
i\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{A}}
with small domain such that the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p(i)
is lifting, and such that, for every
a\in|{\mathbf{A}}|
, the
{\mathbb{V}}
-natural family
\{A(a,|i|a^{\prime}),p(|i|a^{\prime})\Rightarrow p(a)\}_{a^{\prime}\in|{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}|}
formed by the left-action of
p
is left-opcartesian in
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
:

p(a)\cong A(a,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i)

A weight
(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\colon{\mathbf{A}}_{n}{\mathrel{\to}}\cdots{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}_{0}
in
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
is
colimit-small
when the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p_{k}(1,a_{k})
is small for every
1\leq k\leq n
and
a_{k}\in|{\mathbf{A}}_{k}|
.

Remark 9.35
.

??
implies that the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p
in
??
is the left-composite
A(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i)
.

Remark 9.36
.

We say
colimit-small
instead of just
small
because, while we use the same notion of weight for both colimits and limits, colimit-smallness does not coincide with
limit-smallness
(which is colimit-smallness in
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}\cong{\mathbb{V}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
; see
??
).

Remark 9.37

(label=small-flexibility)
.

Small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves are called
accessible
in
[
Kel82
]
(for
{\mathbb{V}}
a symmetric closed monoidal category), while our notion of colimit-small weight is similar to
[
Shu13
]
’s notion of
\kappa
-small profunctor
between enriched indexed categories
[
Shu13
, Definition 10.1]
.
Neither require
i
to be fully faithful, but both authors (
[
Kel82
, Proposition 4.83]
and
[
Shu13
, Remark 10.6]
) show that one can always replace a non-fully faithful
i
with a fully faithful
i
, so that this difference is irrelevant.

\Citeauthor
shulman2013enriched’s proof makes it clear that this fact relies on existence of certain composites; since we do not generally have these composites, we directly require that
i
is fully faithful (for the proof of
??
below).
Moreover, a direct translation of their definitions into our setting would only require the existence of
some

p^{\prime}
(not necessarily
p(i)
) such that
p\cong A(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p^{\prime}
.
Again this distinction is irrelevant (cf.
[
Kel82
, Proposition 4.83]
), since, if
i
is fully faithful, then:

p^{\prime}\cong(A(i,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p^{\prime})\cong(A(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p^{\prime})(i)\cong p(i)

Neither
[
Kel82
]
nor
[
Shu13
]
has an explicit lifting assumption, but nor do they need one: since
p(i)
has small codomain, it is automatically lifting when
{\mathbb{V}}
is locally complete and has right lifts, by
??
.

The main reason for considering small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves is the fact that they are lifting, and hence that their presheaf-objects exist.

Lemma 9.38

(label=small-right-lifts-exist)
.

Every small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf, and every colimit-small weight, is lifting.
In particular, if
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
is a class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors induced by a class of small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves, then every
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object.

Proof.

If
p\cong{\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i)
is a small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf, with
p(i)
lifting, then we have
q(i)\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i)\cong(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\mathbf{A}}(1,i))\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i)\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}({\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i))\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p
.
We prove that every colimit-small weight
\vec{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})
is lifting by induction on
n
.
For
n=0
this is trival.
For
n>0
, it is enough to show that
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\dots,p_{n}(1,b))
exists for all objects
b
by
??
.
This is the case because the small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p_{n}(1,b)
is lifting, and
q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\dots,p_{n-1})\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p_{n}(1,b)\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}(p_{1},\dots,p_{n-1},p_{n}(1,b))
by
??
.

That every
{\mathbb{V}}
-category admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-presheaf object follows from
??
.
∎

Lemma 9.39

(label=colimit-small-composite-lemma)
.

If a unary weight
p\colon{\mathbf{B}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
is colimit-small, then, for every small full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
j\colon{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{B}}
, there is a small full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
i\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{A}}
such that

p(1,j)\cong{\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i,j)

and such that
p(i,j)
is lifting.

Proof.

For every
b\in|{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}|
, since
p(1,|j|b)
is a small
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf, there is some small full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
i_{b}\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}_{b}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{A}}
such that
p(1,|j|b)\cong{\mathbf{A}}(1,i_{b})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{b},|j|b)
, and such that
p(i_{b},|j|b)
is lifting.
Let
i\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}\to{\mathbf{A}}
to be the union of the
i_{a}
; this is a small union, so
{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}
is small.

\textstyle|{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}|=\bigcup_{b\in|{\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}|}|{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}_{b}|

Since each
i_{a}
factors through
i
, the latter witnesses smallness of the
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaf
p(1,|j|b)
for every
b
:

\displaystyle p(1,|j|b)\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}(1,i_{b})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{b},|j|b)

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle({\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\odot{\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b}))\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{b},|j|b)

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}({\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{b},|j|b))

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i,|j|b)

It follows from
??
that
p(1,j)\cong{\mathbf{A}}(1,i)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i,j)
.
To see that
p(i,j)
is lifting, it is enough by
??
to show that
p(i,|j|b)
is lifting for all
b
.
This is the case because
{\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b})
is a companion, and is therefore lifting by
[
AM24
, Example 3.3]
, so we can construct right lifts through

q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i,|j|b)
by the following.

(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b}))\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i_{b},|j|b)\cong(q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}{\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b}))\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i_{b},|j|b)\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}({\mathbf{A}}(i,i_{b})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{b},|j|b))\cong q\mathbin{\blacktriangleleft}p(i,|j|b)\qed

Remark 9.40
.

??
is an adaptation of
[
Shu13
, Lemma 10.7]
to our setting.
Our proof is similar, but subtly different to
[

Proof.

(1) is trivial: we can take
i
to be the identity in the definition of smallness.

For (2), let
i\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{A}}
be the full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of
{\mathbf{A}}
containing only
a
.
Then we have
{\mathbf{A}}(a^{\prime},a)\cong{\mathbf{A}}(a^{\prime},i)\odot{\mathbf{A}}(i,a)
as required.

For (3), we show that there is some
i_{0}\colon{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}_{0}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{A}}_{0}
with small domain, such that

q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p\cong{\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p)(i_{0},1)

and such that
(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p)(i_{0},1)
is lifting.
We have the following, where the full sub-
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories
i_{k}
are provided by
??
, and the associativity laws use the fact that
{\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})
, and each
q_{k}
, is lifting (
??
); they are instances of
??
.

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}({\mathbf{A}}_{m}(1,i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m}))

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}{\mathbf{A}}_{m}(1,i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(1,i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}({\mathbf{A}}_{m-1}(1,i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m}))\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}{\mathbf{A}}_{m-1}(1,i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}(1,i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle\cdots

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle({\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{1}(i_{0},i_{1}))\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}(i_{m-1},i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{1}(i_{0},i_{1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}(i_{m-1},i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

By similar reasoning, we can show that

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{1}(i_{0},i_{1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}(i_{m-1},i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

\displaystyle{\mathbf{A}}_{0}(1,i_{0})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{1}(i_{0},1)\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{2}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p

\displaystyle\penalty\ \cong\penalty\

as required.

q_{1}(i_{0},i_{1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m-1}(i_{m-1},i_{m-1})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}(i_{m-1},i_{m})\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p(i_{m})

??

(q_{1}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{2}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}\cdots\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}q_{m}\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p)(i_{0},1)

8

In fact, it holds more generally for categories enriched in virtual double categories.
, means that it is unnecessary to study
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
specifically, as it is implicitly included in the preceding development.

Proposition 9.46

(label=V^co-Cat)
.

For each virtual bicategory
{\mathbb{V}}
, there is an isomorphism of virtual equipments
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}\cong{\mathbb{V}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
.

Proof.

By inspection.
∎

Consequently, copresheaf objects and free completions in
{{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
are respectively presheaf objects and free cocompletions in
{\mathbb{V}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}\textup{-}\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}
. We therefore immediately obtain construction theorems therefor; for convenience, we spell out the main definitions and results.

Definition
co
.

A class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors is
copresheaf-induced
if a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
p\colon{\mathbf{B}}{\mathrel{\to}}{\mathbf{A}}
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
if and only if, for each
b\in|{\mathbf{B}}|
, the
{\mathbb{V}}
-copresheaf
p(b,1)
is in
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
.

Theorem
co
.

Let
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
be a copresheaf-induced class of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-copresheaf
{\mathbb{V}}
-category if and only if the right extension
p\mathbin{\blacktriangleright}q
exists for all
{\mathbb{V}}
-copresheaves
p,q\in\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
on
{\mathbf{A}}
. In this case,
{\mathbf{A}}
is furthermore
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-coadmissible if and only if the repletion of
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
contains the identity
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor on
{\mathbf{A}}
.

Theorem
co
.

Assume that
{\mathbb{V}}
is locally complete and has right extensions. Every small
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
{\mathbf{A}}
admits a
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
-copresheaf
{\mathbb{V}}
-category, for every copresheaf-induced class
\mathbf{\mathbb{P}}
of
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors.

10.
Context and examples

We conclude by (1) explaining the relationship between our construction of free cocompletions of enriched categories and those appearing in the literature, (2) describing some specific classes of weights of interest in bicategory-enriched category theory, and (3) illustrating these by means of examples of categories enriched in certain bicategories.

10.1.
Historical context

The possibility of freely completing a category under a class
{\mathcal{J}}
of colimits was considered early in the development of category theory. However, it took some time before a general construction was realised; typically, the class
{\mathcal{J}}
was subject to certain compatibility conditions, or the construction was limited to small categories. Below, we provide a survey of constructions that appeared in the literature.

Example 10.4

10.3.
Examples of free cocompletions

To indicate our motivation for providing a general construction of free (co)completions for categories enriched in (virtual) bicategories, we recall some notable examples of (co)completions with regard to specific bases of enrichment.

Example 10.7
.

Let
{\mathbf{C}}
be a small category and denote by
\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}})
the full sub-bicategory of
\mathbf{Rel}({\mathbf{Set}}^{C{}^{\mathrm{op}}})

on
{\mathbf{C}}
are in bijection with locally finitely continuous and identity-on-objects lax endofunctors on

spanned by the

is equivalent to the category of symmetric
\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J)
-enriched categories admitting colimits weighted by left adjoints (
??
)
[
Wal82
, Theorem]
.

Denoting by
J_{0}
the trivial coverage on a small category
{\mathbf{C}}

\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J_{0})\to\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J)
and hence a functor

{\mathbf{Set}}^{{\mathbf{C}}{}^{\mathrm{op}}}\to\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J_{0})\textup{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J)\textup{-}\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{R}({\mathbf{C}},J)\textup{-}\mathbf{Cat}

Example 10.10
.

Let
{\mathbf{B}}
be a locally small category and denote by
{\mathbb{V}}=\Sigma{\mathbf{Set}}/{\mathbf{B}}
the local cocompletion of
{\mathbf{B}}
viewed as a locally discrete 2-category; a 1-cell

{\mathbb{V}}

. The process of forming free fibrations has long been known to exhibit a colax-idempotent pseudomonad

and, conceptually, colax-idempotent pseudomonads correspond to completions under classes of limits. However, the perspective of enrichment in a bicategory shows that this process really is a free completion in the conventional sense. This perspective moreover extends from fibrations of categories to fibrations of enriched categories
[

, Theorem 5.5]

10.4.
A generalised Eilenberg–Watts theorem

In 1960,
[
Eil60
]
and
[
Wat60
]
independently provided a characterisation of those additive functors between categories of modules for rings that are induced by tensoring with a bimodule: this characterisation has come to be known as the
Eilenberg–Watts theorem

[
Eil60
,
Wat60
]
. To conclude, we observe that the theory we have developed herein provides a four-fold generalisation of the classical Eilenberg–Watts theorem.

(10.12.(1))

From enrichment in the category of Abelian groups to enrichment in any well behaved bicategory.

(10.12.(2))

From monoids in a monoidal category (which may be seen as one-object enriched categories) to (many-object) enriched categories.

(10.12.(3))

From a fixed class of weights (namely, the small weights) to an arbitrary class of small weights.

(10.12.(4))

Establishing not merely an equivalence of categories (with respect to the bimodules between two fixed monoids), but a biequivalence of bicategories (permitting the enriched categories to vary).

Theorem 10.13
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a locally complete and left-locally cocomplete bicategory with right lifts, and let
\Phi
be a class of colimit-small weights. The process of left extension and restriction along the embeddings of
\Phi
-cocompletions exhibits a biequivalence between

•

the bicategory whose objects are
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories, for which a 1-cell from
\mathbf{A}
to
\mathbf{B}
is a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor

\mathbf{A}\to{\widehat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{B})
from
\mathbf{A}
to the
\Phi
-cocompletion of
{\mathbf{B}}
, and whose 2-cells are
{\mathbb{V}}

Appendix A
Local (co)completeness of virtual double categories

In this appendix, we introduce the notions of local limits and local colimits in virtual double categories, necessary to establish the existence of free cocompletions of enriched categories in
??
, and establish the relation to local limits and local colimits in bicategories. Since virtual double categories are not closed under the reversal of tight-cells (since 2-cells have multiary domain but unary codomain), the notion of local limit is
not
dual to the notion of local colimit. Consequently, their specialisations to bicategories are also not dual: local limits, in contrast to local colimits, are not required to be stable under composition.

A.1.
Local limits

Definition A.1
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a virtual double category, let
A,B
be objects of
\mathbb{X}
, and let
p\colon\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{X}\llbracket B,A\rrbracket
be a functor between categories. A
local limit
of
p
comprises the following data.

(A.1.(1))

A loose-cell
\lim p\colon B{\mathrel{\to}}A
.

(A.1.(2))

For each
j\in\mathbf{J}
, a globular 2-cell
\pi_{j}\colon\lim p\Rightarrow p_{j}
. Furthermore, for each
\jmath\colon j\to j^{\prime}
in
\mathbf{J}
, the following equation should hold.

A functor
F\colon\mathbb{X}\to\mathbb{Y}
of virtual double category
preserves
the local limit if the induced loose-cell
F(\lim p)
together with the family
\{F(\pi_{j})\}_{j\in\mathbf{J}}
exhibits a local limit of
F_{B,A}\circ p\colon\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{Y}\llbracket FB,FA\rrbracket
.

Let
{\mathcal{J}}
be a class of categories. A virtual double category is
locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) complete
if it admits all (
(\mathbf{J}\in{\mathcal{J}})
-indexed) local limits; a functor is
locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) continuous
if it preserves all (
(\mathbf{J}\in{\mathcal{J}})
-indexed) local limits.

Note that, since the notion of local limit is symmetric with respect to the loose-cells, a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
is locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) complete if and only if
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
(
??
) is locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) complete.

Remark A.2
.

A pseudo double category admits local products in the sense of
[
Pat26
, Example 6.10]
if and only if, when viewed as a representable virtual double category, it admits local
{\mathcal{J}}
-limits, for
{\mathcal{J}}
the class of discrete categories.

Lemma A.3
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a virtual equipment.
\mathbb{X}
admits the local limit of a functor
p\colon\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{X}\llbracket B,A\rrbracket
if and only if the loose virtual bicategory underlying
\mathbb{X}
admits a local limit of
p
.

Proof.

Clearly data (1 & 2) do not depend on tight-cells in
\mathbb{X}
. For each family of 2-cells in
\mathbb{X}
,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{j}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\chi_{j}}

we have a family of globular 2-cells in
\mathbb{X}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A(1,x)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B(x^{\prime},1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{j}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widecheck{\chi_{j}}}

Since
p
admits a local limit in the loose virtual bicategory, we have a 2-cell as follows,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A(1,x)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B(x^{\prime},1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lim p}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle\widecheck{\chi_{j}}\rangle_{j\in\mathbf{J}}}

hence a 2-cell as follows, where
\urcorner
and
\ulcorner
are the evident 2-cells induced by the universal property of restriction.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A(1,x)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q_{n}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle\widecheck{\chi_{j}}\rangle_{j\in\mathbf{J}}}

This satisfies the desired universal property by the universal property for the local limit in the loose bicategory together with the universal property of the restriction. The converse is trivial.
∎

Proposition A.4
.

Each hom-category of a bicategory is
{\mathcal{J}}
-complete if and only if the bicategory, when viewed as the loose bicategory of a representable virtual double category, admits local
{\mathcal{J}}
-limits in the sense of
??
.

Proof.

In the presence of loose-composites, it is clear that, in the universal property of a local limit (
A.1.(3)
), it suffices to consider unary 2-cells. The universal property is then precisely that of a limit in the hom-category.
∎

A functor
F\colon\mathbb{X}\to\mathbb{Y}
of virtual double category
preserves
the local colimit if the induced loose-cell
F(\colim p)
together with the family
\{F(\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{j})\}_{j\in\mathbf{J}}
exhibits a local colimit of
F_{B,A}\circ p\colon\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{Y}\llbracket FB,FA\rrbracket
.

Let
{\mathcal{J}}
be a class of categories. A virtual double category is
locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) cocomplete
if it admits all (
(\mathbf{J}\in{\mathcal{J}})
-indexed) local colimits; a functor is
locally (
{\mathcal{J}}
-) cocontinuous
if it preserves all (
(\mathbf{J}\in{\mathcal{J}})
-indexed) local colimits.

Definition A.6
.

A
weak local colimit
satisfies the universal property of
??
only when
k=0
and
n=0
and
x
and
x^{\prime}
are identities. A
left-local colimit
satisfies the universal property only when
k=0
and
x
is an identity, and dually for
right-local colimits
. A virtual double category is
weakly locally cocomplete
,
left-locally cocomplete
, or
right-locally cocomplete
if it admits all weak local colimits, left-local colimits, or right-local colimits respectively.

(A
weak local colimit
should be distinguished from a
local weak colimit
, which satisfies only the existence aspect of the universal property, but nevertheless satisfies this existence property with respect to multiary 2-cells.) Note that a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
admits (left) local colimits if and only if
\mathbb{X}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
(
??
) admits (right) local colimits.

The following extends an observation in
[
Par13
, Remark 2.1.2]
from double categories to virtual double categories.

Lemma A.7
.

Let
\mathbb{X}
be a virtual double category with restrictions.
\mathbb{X}
admits the local colimit of a functor
p\colon\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{X}\llbracket B,A\rrbracket
if and only if the loose virtual bicategory underlying
\mathbb{X}
admits a local colimit of
p
.

Proposition A.8
.

If
\mathbb{X}
admits loose-composites, then the following are equivalent.

(A.8.(1))

\mathbb{X}
admits a local colimit of
p
.

(A.8.(2))

\mathbb{X}
admits a weak local colimit of
p
, and
\colim p
is preserved by pre- and post-whiskering of loose-cells, in the sense that the canonical 2-cell
r\odot p_{j}\odot s\Rightarrow r\odot\colim p\odot s
induced by the following 2-cell exhibits the coprojection at
j\in\mathbf{J}
of a colimit of
\mathbf{J}\to\mathbb{X}\llbracket B,A\rrbracket\to\mathbb{X}\llbracket S,R\rrbracket
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{j}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\shortmid}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\colim p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r\odot\colim p\odot s}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\scriptstyle\pi$}}_{j}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}

Remark A.9

(label=left-composites-and-whiskering)
.

More generally, if
\mathbb{X}
admits left-composites, then
\mathbb{X}
admits a left-local colimit of
p
if and only if
\mathbb{X}
admits a weak local colimit of
p
, and
\colim p
is preserved by pre-whiskering of loose-cells, in the sense that the canonical 2-cell
p_{j}\odot s\Rightarrow\colim p\odot s
exhibits the coprojection at
j\in{\mathcal{J}}
.
